commenti.body:
The Criterion Collection does not include Mr. Herzog's **Fitzcarraldo**.  Criterion has a documentary about the making of that film called **Burden of Dreams** by Les Blank.

It's a great movie, I'm sure the version on Amazon Prime is just fine.

Was my least favorite of the full length non documentary movies i watched of his in a film class about him, seems like a much better story of how it got made than an actual product that sticks with me.

All of his films are challenging, and demand that you shed your expectations/ideas about what Herzog is all about. Fitzcarraldo is primarily a lighthearted comedy, which is not his usual approach and is probably what throws people. It's also one of his most slowly paced films. You have to be ready to just soak in the visuals and not worry about getting through the story.

From a purely personal perspective, I didn’t like Fitzcarraldo…

… however, *Embrace of the Serpent* is an absolutely fantastic film and I understood it so much more after watching Fitzcarraldo.

So whether you enjoy Fitzcarraldo or not, watch Embrace of the Serpent! It will retroactively make you appreciate Fitzcarraldo more.

I'll assume that you've finished by now, but...

They did not record audio on set, and not all of the actors spoke German. I'm pretty sure the English soundtrack includes more of the actual actors than the German track.

If the Herzog movies you watched were like *Aguirre*, then I can't think of why you wouldn't like *Fitzcarraldo*. It's one of his more popular fiction films, even if it is the longest. It is a bit less accessible than his popular documentaries (it's slower, more ambiguous, not as quirky), but if you've seen more than a few of those, then you should be fine.

If you did finish it, I'm interested to hear what you thought. Ditto on if your friend shared anything more about it.

I prefer burden of dreams which is the documentary about a madman trying to get a boat over a mountain rather than fitzcarraldo which is the “fiction” film about a madman trying to get a boat over a mountain. But it only works if you watch both films about a madmen trying to get a boat over a mountain.

Best to make opinions yourself, no matter how much you trust someone else's. Herzog is an artist that is after something in particular, a thing he calls the "ecstatic truth", or the reality of our world that only cinema can communicate. He does not distinguish between documentary or fiction, and often his films are a product of both.

*Fitzcarraldo* is one of the best representatives of this mindset, because it was a miracle in and of itself that it was even made; almost everything you see in the film was as much a struggle as it appears to be, and that aspect alone encapsulates the narrative of the film. It might seem simplistic to suggest that a man's obsessive vision to build an opera house in the jungle is anything revolutionary, but the ambition of this idea intersects with the doubts and fears Herzog had himself as a filmmaker, enriching its narrative through autobiographical parallels.

There is poetry in the notion that both Herzog and Fitzcarraldo persevere, and both have to contend with defeat. Even if you "build the opera house", there are no guarantees anyone will see the tremendous effort that went into its construction. It's entirely possible no one will ever know the beauty you see in art, whatever that might mean to you, and as such they will never appreciate the sacrifice it took to make it, nor the passing of time that renders such ambition unnecessary in hindsight, save for everyone but those that care to remember it. 

*Fitzcarraldo* will forever be exemplary of the problems we face as human beings, and from my perspective, that's what makes it an important film.

Oh honey, just dive in! Herzog is a ride no matter the language. Yes, watching in the original language is usually ideal, but don't let that stress you out. The heart of Fitzcarraldo is in its audacity and vision. Fret less, watch more, and let Herzog work his magic. You're in for an adventure! ❤️
I always tell folks to watch 'Burden of Dreams' *first* before tackling 'Fitzcarraldo'. It literally makes it a different film. (And maybe 'My Best Fiend' for the adventurous.)
